title: GLM-5.3 vs. GPT-5.6 Sol on DeepSWE: Cost, Coding, and Routing
gist: On Together AI's DeepSWE benchmark, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol edges GLM-5.3 on single-shot coding accuracy and is far faster, but the two models diverge enough (0.43 correlation) that cascading GLM-5.3 first and escalating to Sol beats either model alone, reaching 85.9% accuracy at $6.61 per task versus Sol's 72.7% at $8.37.

themes.theme: Single-shot accuracy and the flagship's remaining edge

insights.claim: GPT-5.6 Sol scores 72.7% pass@1 on DeepSWE versus GLM-5.3's 69.0%, a 3.7 point gap the authors describe as sitting inside a couple of standard deviations, meaning Sol retains the single-shot accuracy crown but only narrowly.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: A shrinking single-shot accuracy gap between a closed OpenAI flagship and an open-weight challenger signals continued compression of the frontier moat on coding tasks specifically.
insights.quote: Sol wins the single shot, narrowly. 72.7% pass@1 against GLM-5.3's 69.0%, a 3.7 point gap that sits inside a couple of standard deviations.

insights.claim: GPT-5.6 Sol solves more tasks perfectly across all four trials than GLM-5.3 (61 vs. 48) and posts higher per-attempt reliability (84.5% vs. 78.8%), making it the more consistent, precision-oriented model.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: For single-attempt, high-stakes coding tasks where retries aren't practical, Sol's higher reliability is a legitimate reason to pay its premium rather than defaulting to the cheaper model.
insights.quote: Sol is the precision corner: 84.5% reliability and 61 tasks solved four for four, the marks of a model that lands what it touches.

insights.claim: GLM-5.3 ties GPT-5.6 Sol at pass@2 (81.1% vs. 81.0%) and overtakes it at pass@4 (87.6% vs. 85.8%), meaning the open model has the wider reach once multiple attempts are allowed, at half of Sol's per-attempt cost.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: In any best-of-k or retry-tolerant coding-agent deployment, GLM-5.3 becomes the more accurate choice as well as the cheaper one, undercutting the case for defaulting to GPT-5.6 Sol in agentic pipelines.
insights.quote: The open model has the wider reach, so in any best-of-k setting it is the more accurate choice, and its extra attempts cost half of Sol's.

insights.claim: GLM-5.3 achieves higher coverage (87.6% of tasks solved at least once) than GPT-5.6 Sol (85.8%), trading off lower per-attempt reliability (78.8% vs. 84.5%) and fewer solid four-for-four solves (48 vs. 61) for broader reach across the benchmark.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: Coverage vs. reliability is a distinct tradeoff axis from raw pass@1; teams building retry-based agent loops should weight coverage more heavily than single-shot precision, favoring GLM-5.3.
insights.quote: GLM-5.3 touches more of the benchmark than Sol and converts each touch a little less often per shot.

themes.theme: Cost, speed, and the routing cascade

insights.claim: GLM-5.3 costs $3.99 per rollout versus $8.37 for GPT-5.6 Sol, a 2.1x price gap, translating to 17 solved tasks per $100 spent for GLM-5.3 versus 9 for Sol.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: A roughly 2x price advantage with near-parity accuracy is a direct competitive argument for Together AI-served open-weight inference over OpenAI's flagship for cost-sensitive, high-volume coding workloads.
insights.quote: The price gap is 2.1x. $3.99 per rollout against $8.37. Per $100 spent, GLM-5.3 solves 17 tasks and Sol solves 9.

insights.claim: GPT-5.6 Sol is dramatically faster and more concise: 19 minutes and 61 steps per rollout versus GLM-5.3's 35 minutes and 124 steps, with lower output token usage (60k vs. 80k), so Sol earns its premium primarily on latency rather than accuracy.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: For latency-sensitive, human-in-the-loop coding assistants, Sol's roughly 2x speed advantage may justify its price even absent an accuracy edge; for batch/asynchronous workloads GLM-5.3's cost edge dominates instead.
insights.quote: If a human is waiting, Sol earns its premium on latency alone. If a budget or a batch queue is waiting, GLM-5.3 is the better buy.

insights.claim: A cascade that runs GLM-5.3 first and escalates to GPT-5.6 Sol only when tests fail solves 85.9% of DeepSWE tasks at $6.61 per task — thirteen points more accurate than Sol alone (72.7%) and cheaper than a single Sol rollout ($8.37).
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: This cascade pattern (cheap open-weight model first, expensive closed model as verifier-gated escalation) is a concrete, quantified blueprint for cutting inference costs while beating either single model's accuracy — directly actionable for any team building coding agents.
insights.quote: That cascade solves 85.9% of DeepSWE tasks at $6.61 each. Sol alone solves 72.7% at $8.37. Thirteen points better, 21% cheaper.

insights.claim: The GLM-first cascade even beats a theoretical perfect one-shot oracle router (83.8% accuracy), because two independent attempts from divergent models outperform one perfect single pick.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: This is a non-obvious result: sequential cascading of two only-moderately-correlated models can outperform even a perfect classifier-based router, an important architectural insight for teams building model-routing infrastructure rather than just picking a single best model.
insights.quote: The cascade also beats a perfect one-shot oracle router (83.8%), because two independent attempts beat one perfect pick.

insights.claim: Expected cascade accuracy is the same regardless of which model leads, but leading with GLM-5.3 is cheaper ($6.61 vs. $9.47 if Sol leads), so the authors recommend always leading with the lower-cost model in a cascade.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: A generalizable rule for cascade design: order by cost, not by capability, since accuracy is order-independent but cost is not — directly applicable to any multi-model routing system.
insights.quote: Expected accuracy is the same whichever model leads, but GLM-first is cheaper ($6.61 against $9.47), so lead with the lower-cost model.

insights.claim: GPT-5.6 Sol breaks previously-passing tests (regresses) in 20% of its failures, which the authors call 'the GPT-family regression signature,' versus just 11% for GLM-5.3, meaning GLM-5.3's failures are cleaner and safer to accept without heavy verification gating.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: A near-2x regression rate for Sol implies teams deploying it need heavier automated regression-testing infrastructure around its output, an operational cost not captured in the raw per-token price.
insights.quote: GLM-5.3's failures are cleaner. It breaks tests that already passed in 11% of its failures, against 20% for Sol. Gate Sol's diffs on regressions.

insights.claim: GPT-5.6 Sol and GLM-5.3 split the eight task domains evenly, four wins each; Sol dominates exact-contract, systems-heavy work (data modeling/serialization 92%, build/ops 73%, concurrency/durability 72%, protocol conformance 59%), while GLM-5.3 leads structured, interpreter-style work (query/config 88%, runtime internals 83%, stateful reactivity 73%).
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: The even domain split (unlike GLM-5.3's 5-3 domain win over Claude Fable 5 in a separate comparison) shows GPT-5.6 Sol is a stronger, more broadly capable competitor than other models GLM-5.3 has been benchmarked against.
insights.quote: Sol has no single weak domain; it is simply strong across the board.
insights.locator: Where each wins, by task type

insights.claim: GLM-5.3's weakest domain against GPT-5.6 Sol is protocol conformance at 44%, 15 points behind Sol's 59%, identified as GLM-5.3's one clear hole in this matchup.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: Protocol-conformance-heavy workloads are a specific case where routing to GPT-5.6 Sol over GLM-5.3 is justified despite the general cost/coverage advantage of GLM-5.3.
insights.quote: GLM-5.3's one clear hole is protocol conformance at 44%, 15 points behind Sol.
insights.locator: Where each wins, by task type

insights.claim: GLM-5.3 posts the best JavaScript score of any model on the board at 90%, 15 points ahead of GPT-5.6 Sol's 75%, and also leads Rust 70% to 60%; Sol answers with Python (74% vs. 66%), Go (79% vs. 76%), and TypeScript (66% vs. 61%).
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: GLM-5.3's repeated best-in-class JavaScript performance (also seen versus Claude Fable 5) is a consistent, cross-comparison competitive marker for JS/web-focused coding-agent product routing decisions.
insights.quote: GLM-5.3's standout is JavaScript at 90%, 15 points clear of Sol's 75 and the best JS number of any model on the board.
insights.locator: GLM-5.3 vs. GPT-5.6 Sol by programming language

insights.claim: GLM-5.3 and GPT-5.6 Sol have a per-task correlation of only 0.43 — real disagreement between two models close on aggregate accuracy — and their union covers 106 of 113 tasks (93.8%), which is what makes the escalation cascade effective.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: Low correlation (0.43) versus a much higher correlation (0.65) seen between GLM-5.3 and Claude Fable 5 in a companion comparison shows GPT-5.6 Sol is a genuinely more complementary pairing for portfolio/ensemble routing than Fable is.
insights.quote: Different enough to route on. Per-task correlation is 0.43, real disagreement for two models this close on aggregate.
insights.locator: How different are GLM-5.3 and GPT-5.6 Sol?

insights.claim: GLM-5.3 sweeps (solves 4-for-4) two specific tasks that GPT-5.6 Sol never lands (koota-pair-relation-tracking and participle-grammar-conflict-analysis), while Sol sweeps zero tasks that GLM-5.3 completely fails, indicating the open model reaches places the flagship does not.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: Asymmetric task coverage (GLM-5.3 has exclusive wins that Sol cannot replicate under any of four attempts) undercuts the assumption that a closed frontier model strictly dominates an open-weight challenger, even in categories the flagship generally wins.
insights.quote: GLM-5.3 sweeps two tasks four for four that Sol never lands ... while Sol sweeps none that GLM-5.3 zeros. The open model reaches places the flagship does not.
insights.locator: How different are GLM-5.3 and GPT-5.6 Sol?

insights.claim: The authors frame GLM-5.3 as 'the open-weight challenger that closed the gap' against GPT-5.6 Sol, describing this comparison as 'the closest the open tier has come to the frontier,' explicitly positioning open-weight models as converging on closed frontier lab performance.
insights.speaker: Zain Hasan, Shobhit Dixit
insights.so_what: This is a direct market-narrative claim about the open-weight vs. closed-model competitive gap narrowing, relevant to any investor tracking whether proprietary LLM labs retain a durable moat on coding-specific capability.
insights.quote: This is the closest the open tier has come to the frontier, and the question worth answering is what Sol's remaining premium actually buys.
